promptHead: Athlete goal: 5K (Corrowmore Harvest 5K) on Sun Nov 15 2026, 3 weeks out, target run the whole way.

new.headline: Restart this week one step below your last session, not from zero. You can realistically finish the 5K on Nov 15 with run blocks and short walks, but running it the whole way is a stretch.

flags.title: Two weeks off

flags.title: Whole-way goal
flags.detail: Your longest unbroken run is 2 minutes. Running the whole 5K on Nov 15 is unlikely, so I'm planning run blocks with short walks. We review this after the week of Oct 26 – Nov 1.

flags.title: Sleep and stress
flags.detail: Sleep averaged 6 hrs with high stress. If a morning is too much, shorten the run or skip it. Do not double up or make a missed run up later.

answers.question: I haven't run for two weeks. Do I have to start again from the beginning? And is the 5K in four weeks still realistic?
answers.answer:
No, you do not need to start from the beginning. Two weeks off costs very little fitness, and your last run was 24 minutes of 2 minutes running and 1 minute walking on Sat Oct 3. This week restarts one step below that and builds back up.

Finishing the Corrowmore Harvest 5K on Sun Nov 15 is realistic. Running the whole way without walking is unlikely this time, because your longest unbroken run is 2 minutes and a 5K at your pace takes about 40 to 45 minutes. A better race plan is runs of about 5 minutes with 1 minute walks, extending a block whenever you feel good.

Running the whole way stays your goal, but I would move it to a later 5K after six or so steady weeks. If you would rather keep it for Nov 15, tell me and I will keep building toward it.

new.analysis:
Your fitness has dipped only a little, and what limits you now is steady weeks rather than speed. Runs happened in only three of the last six weeks, first because work got busy and then because of your mum. I'm glad she is home. A runner this new gains most from three short, easy sessions every week, so that is all this week asks.

The calendar says these are the sharpening weeks before the race, which would normally mean faster running. That does not fit you. Your limit is how long you can keep jogging, not how fast, so every session stays easy and the only progress is longer run blocks. A hard session now would add tiredness without helping you finish.

Slowing down is what lets the blocks grow. A pace you can hold for 2 minutes at effort 6 will not last 5 minutes, but a talking pace will. Over a 5K the walk breaks already set your average pace, so jogging slower costs you only a minute or two.

If this week goes to plan, the next step is blocks of 3 to 4 minutes. After that come blocks of 5 or 6 minutes in the week of Nov 2 – 8, and race week is short and easy. Move up only when the sessions felt easy. One rough week means repeating a step, not skipping ahead.

Sleep and stress make every run feel harder, so a shorter run or a skipped morning is a fine call. Walking the dog most days already gives you easy movement, and it is enough on the rest days. A bit of stiffness from driving should ease in the first few minutes of jogging. If it turns into pain that builds as you run, stop and see a physio.

settingsProposalBullets: Family commitments (your mum's hospital stay, now home) interrupted training in early October, so plan a short fallback session for busy weeks.
Treat finishing the Nov 15 5K with run blocks and short walks as the race goal, and running the whole way as the next target, unless you tell me otherwise.
Run blocks should feel like effort 4 to 5 out of 10, a pace where you can speak in full sentences.
